content.title: Notebook Underwood eyeing more Twins Ivisic lineup for different look Preparing for Purdue
content.text: Underwood wanted to play the twin Ivisic lineup more against Maryland, but Zvonimir Ivisic's foul trouble limited that.CHAMPAIGN — Brad Underwood didn't want to remodel the house without Kylan Boswell, but he knew Illinois would need to do some temporary renovation without its fixture in the rotation.A full-scale makeover would be too disruptive to an Illini team that's won eight straight games, is among the top-12 teams in the country and one that will get Boswell, the star guard out with a broken right hand, back in "three to four weeks" following Thursday's surgery.Underwood has been here before during his Illini tenure. Star players — Ayo Dosunmu, Terrence Shannon Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, Tomislav Ivisic — have missed a handful of games here or there during Underwood's rebuilding of the basketball program. The answer in all of those instances has been to adjust just a few things to keep the flow and basic principles of the program while allowing for a seamless return to action.In Wednesday's home win over Maryland, Underwood wanted to go bigger against the Terrapins. The Illini head coach has more and more been experimenting with a double Ivisic lineup, putting twins Tomislav Ivisic and Zvonimir Ivisic on the floor at the same time. No Boswell for the time being further opened that door.It just didn't happen.Zvonimir Ivisic got in early foul trouble with a personal and a Flagrant 1 foul in his first 1:17 on the court, and he missed most of the first half. That continued in the second half when he picked up a second Flagrant 1 foul — players can get three before being ejected — and played just nine minutes."I wanted to play bigger longer," Underwood said. "I didn't get to do that. I think we have some advantages in size, and I was curious to see [Wednesday] how that would look," Underwood said. "...We figured [the Terrapins] were going to play some zone. LoginIllini icon Dee Brown reveling in Illinois Final Four run: 'This is a great moment to be an Illini'Now the head coach at Division-II Roosevelt University, Brown is jubilant to see Illinois break a two-decade Final Four drought In the two decades since he graced the covers of several national magazines as the face of Illinois basketball's last Final Four team, Dee Brown had seen the gear of too many other Big Ten schools, like Michigan, Ohio State and Michigan State, walking around Chicago.But with Illinois back in the Final Four for the first time in 21 years, the Illini icon — who is now the head coach of Division-II Roosevelt University — is seeing a lot more orange, hearing a lot more I-L-L chants and just witnessing a lot more Illini pride in the Chicago streets."Unbelievable. It's amazing," Brown told Illini Inquirer. "…There's a lot of living alum that's up here and that loves Illinois basketball. So it's a great time to be an alum, great time to be an Illini. I just feel so much joy and happiness that when I'm around [the fans]. It comes out of them too, with the hugs and the high fives."Brown said that roar of the crowd is the thing he misses most about playing for Illinois, but he's happy to see an Illini team receive roars like the iconic 2004-05 team that went 37-2 and made it all the way to the national championship game before a 75-70 loss to North Carolina in St. Louis.That team — led by Brown (an All-American), All-American guard Deron Williams, All-American guard Luther Head, forward Roger Powell Jr. and center James Augustine — was treated like rock stars in the state as they started 29-0 before losing the regular season finale at Ohio State on Matt Sylvester's buzzer beater. They further established themselves as legends with one of the most improbable comebacks in NCAA Tournament history, overcoming a 15-point deficit against Arizona in the Elite Eight to force overtime before winning 90-89 to advance to the program's first Final Four since 1989.That team was so popular that it had to enter the back door of hotels and restaurants for its own security. The bus ride home from Rosemont after the Elite Eight win took four to five hours, Brown said, because fans were lined up to get a glimpse of the iconic team.He's happy to see another Illini team create so many great memories for a passionate fan base, which showed up by the thousands at Willard Airport on Sunday to welcome them home from Houston following its 71-59 win over Iowa in the Elite Eight.To read this full article and more, subscribe now —SALE:75% off first yearGet access to this article and all of the in-depth coverage from the 247Sports Network with this special offer.Join at 75% off AnnualAlready a subscriber? LoginDespite small role, Mihailo Petrovic making most of time with Illini: 'He's been an unbelievable teammate'Petrovic has appeared in 19 games this season.HOUSTON — Mihailo Petrovic is no stranger to top-level competition, but getting to college basketball and getting a front-row look at an experienced college basketball player in Kylan Boswell and an NBA Draft lottery pick in Keaton Wagler took some adjusting.Of course, Petrovic had plenty of adjusting to do in moving across the world at 22 years old, needing to learn more of the English language and walking into a college basketball program that had postseason expectations that it has since met. Add a few injuries (a preseason hamstring and an ankle injury), and Petrovic's role on the Illini never fully manifested, especially with the rise of Wagler as a Big Ten star."I had really tough moments for me because I'm not playing, but I'm trying to do my best to help the team win," Petrovic said. "I had two injuries, so I think those injuries (brought) me back down. I am trying to do my best to give my 100% to teammates."Petrovic has appeared in 19 games this season and is averaging 5.8 minutes and 1.6 points per game, largely with the game already decided. His best game was a 12-point, four-assist game against UTRGV but also gave Illinois a late first-half surge in a home win against Minnesota in which he scored four points in six minutes.
